# Comorbidities in multiple myeloma and implications on survival: A population-based study

Ingigerður S. Sverrisdóttir (1); Sölvi Rögnvaldsson (1); Sigrún Thorsteinsdottir (1); Gauti K. Gíslason (1); Thor Aspelund (1); Ingemar Turesson (2); Magnus Björkholm (3); Henrik Gregersen (4); Cecilie Hveding Blimark (5); Ola Landgren (6); Sigurður Y. Kristinsson (1,7)

## Abstract

High proportion of patients with multiple myeloma suffer from comorbidities which may alter clinical management. Therefore, our aims were to evaluate the prevalence of comorbidities and their impact on survival. We included patients diagnosed with multiple myeloma 1990-2013 in Sweden and all diagnoses from each patient from 1985. A total of 13 656 patients with multiple myeloma were included in the study, thereof 7404 (54%) had comorbidity at diagnosis. The risk of death was increased for those with one comorbidity at diagnosis compared to those without any comorbidity (hazard ratio = 1.19; 95% confidence interval:1.14-1.25); this risk was higher for those with two (1.38; 1.30-1.47) and three or more comorbidities (1.72; 1.62-1.83). Furthermore, the risk of death was increased in patients with prior history of cancer, arrhythmia, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, cerebrovascular disease, chronic lung disease, psychological disease, peptic ulcer, neurological disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic kidney disease, dementia, and inflammatory bowel disease. This large study shows that over 50% of multiple myeloma patients have a comorbidity at diagnosis and survival decreased with increasing numbers of comorbidities. This emphasizes the importance of comorbidities when evaluating patients and deciding on treatment strategies for individuals with multiple myeloma.

**Keywords:** comorbidities, multiple myeloma, survival

## 1 Introduction

Multiple myeloma (MM) is a plasma-cell malignancy that affects approximately 160,000 individuals annually world-wide. \[1\] The median age at diagnosis is around 70 years, 5%-10% of patients are diagnosed below 50 years of age, with a lower prevalence of young patients in population-based studies. \[2,3\] With an aging population and prolonged survival, the incidence and prevalence of MM are increasing \[4-7\] and elderly patients are more likely to suffer from comorbid conditions. \[8,9\]

Comorbidities may influence cancer detection, treatment, progression, and thereby prognosis of each patient. \[10,11\] In MM patients, comorbid diseases may lead to lower performance status, decreased quality of life, and life-threatening conditions. \[12,13\] We have recently shown that concurrent autoimmune disease and thrombosis is associated with inferior survival in MM patients. \[14,15\] Despite the importance of considering comorbid diseases in the treatment and prognosis of MM, the literature on comorbidity in MM is limited and based on small numbers. \[16-20\]

New therapeutic agents with different mechanisms of action, such as lenalidomide, pomalidomide, daratumumab, and carfilzomib, \[21\] have been shown to improve survival in randomized clinical trials (RCTs); however, there are very few clinical trials where elderly and frail patients are included. \[12\] Patients with comorbidities are typically not eligible for enrollment in clinical trials, and, consequently, there is limited information available on comorbidities in MM and implications on clinical outcomes. Therefore, it is of great importance to evaluate comorbidity in MM, in particular using real-world data.

Aims of our study were to evaluate the prevalence of comorbidity and the effect of comorbid conditions on survival in a whole population using real-world data among more than 13 000 newly diagnosed MM patients in Sweden over a period of 23 years.

## 2 Methods

### 2.1 Cohort and registries

All residents of Sweden are, at birth or immigration, assigned a unique personal identification number that is used in government-maintained nationwide health care and population registers, whereby medical record linkage is possible with a high degree of accuracy.

The Swedish Cancer Registry is a centralized, nationwide registry that contains information on patients diagnosed with a malignant disorder in Sweden since January 1, 1958 (completeness >93% for MM patients). \[22\] Using this registry, patients diagnosed with MM from January 1, 1990, to December 31, 2013, were identified.

Using International Code of Diseases (ICD)-10 and ICD-9 codes, a total of 21 disease groups were identified (Table S1). The formation of these groups is explained below. Information on each patient was gathered from the Swedish Patient registry, which contains inpatient data from 1987 as well as information on outpatient visits from 2000. \[23\] All chronic diseases that were diagnosed up to 10 years before the diagnosis of MM were included in the analysis. Diagnosis of comorbid diseases had to be made before the MM diagnosis or a maximum of 30 days after diagnosis with the exception of inflammatory bowel disease, renal, and rheumatological disease. These conditions had to be diagnosed at least half a year before as symptoms of MM might mimic these diseases and lead to a wrong diagnosis. In a sensitivity analysis, we removed all diagnosis up to four weeks prior to the MM diagnosis and risk estimates for each disease remained the same (data not shown). Information on prior cancer diagnoses was obtained from the Swedish Cancer Registry. All cancer diagnoses up to 10 years prior to diagnosis of MM were identified, excluding benign tumors as well as cancer in situ.

End of follow-up was December 31, 2013. The study period was divided into two calendar periods, 1990-1999 and 2000-2013, before and after the introduction of novel treatment options for MM in Sweden. \[6,24\] Information on date of death as well as cause of death was obtained from the centralized Swedish Cause of Death Registry. In evaluating the cause of death, the data were split into those who had MM listed as any cause of death and those without a MM diagnosis in the Cause of Death Registry.

### 2.2 Comorbidity

A total of 65 diseases were identified using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes from the Swedish Patient Registry, using both inpatient and outpatient data. These diseases were grouped together according to previously published data, both the Charlson comorbidity index as well as newly published study from Denmark. \[19,25\] Certain diseases that are not evaluated in the Charlson index were added to capture as many comorbidities as possible, specifically those known to effect survival in the general population as well as the survival of patients with known cancer. \[14,26-31\] In total, psychological disorders, neurological conditions, arrhythmias, pancreatic disease, inflammatory bowel disease, hypertension, and obesity were added. The diseases listed were chronic in nature and typically need lifelong follow-up or treatment.

ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes were used to identify each diagnosis in the corresponding groups, and these codes were based on ICD-9 and ICD-10 versions of the Charlson index. \[32\] In order to group these 65 diseases together, we conducted a separate analysis where all 65 diseases were evaluated independently for their risk of death. Diseases were grouped together according to their ICD-10 classification as well as the organ or organ systems that were affected by the disease. After ICD and organ system classification, diseases were grouped together if the risk of death was similar. A disease was only added to a group if the risk was alike or did not change when the disease was added to that specific category. Altogether, a total of 21 disease groups were defined. Table S1 shows the diseases groups and which diagnosis were included with corresponding ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes for each group.

### 2.3 Statistical analysis

We estimated the effect of comorbidities on the risk of death for patients with MM using two different Cox regression models. The first model included only the number of comorbidities present at diagnosis and the second model included all of the 21 comorbidities we identified. Both models were adjusted for age, sex, and year of diagnosis with age and year of diagnosis as continuous variables. Results were presented as hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Kaplan-Meier curves were used to estimate survival with respect to the number of comorbidities present at diagnosis.

We also looked at all subjects that died during the study period, and cross-linked them to the Cause of Death Registry. Using logistic regression, we evaluated the odds of dying from other causes than MM depending on the number of comorbidities present at diagnosis, with the same adjustment variables as above. Results were presented as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

As the outpatient diagnosis was only available from the year 2000, a sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate if there was any difference in the risk of each comorbidity between two calendar periods, 1990-1999 and 2000-2013. This was done by adding an interaction term between each comorbidity and the time period variable to the Cox model. For further comparison, we fitted a separate Cox model only on inpatient diagnoses to evaluate if the hazard ratios changed when outpatient diagnoses were excluded. To assess the interaction between the risk of each comorbidity and age at diagnosis, we stratified the group into patients older and younger than 70 years of age and fitted a Cox model for each age group separately as well as adding an interaction term between each comorbidity and the age group variable.

Statistical significance was set at P < .05, all confidence intervals were 95%, and all statistical analyses were performed in R version 3.6.1.

## 3 Results

In total, 13 656 patients were diagnosed with MM in the Swedish Cancer Registry from the January 1, 1990, to the December 31, 2013. The median age of diagnosis was 72 years (20-99), and 7481 (54.8%) were male. Around 60% of patients were older than 70 years at the time of MM diagnosis, and 63% of these older patients had a comorbidity at diagnosis (Table 1).

A total of 7404 (54.2%) patients had one or more comorbidity at MM diagnosis, and the most common comorbidities were hypertension (20.4%), cancer (11.3%), arrhythmia (11.3%), and chronic ischemic heart disease (9.2%). Other comorbidities and their prevalence are shown in Figure 1. Of all patients, 3355 (24.6%) had only one comorbidity listed at the MM diagnosis, 1922 (14.1%) had two comorbidities, and 2126 (15.6%) had three or more comorbidities at diagnosis. More patients were diagnosed with MM and concurrent comorbidities during the calendar period 2000-2013 (61.7%) compared to 1990-1999 (38.3%), and patients with comorbidities were older at the time of MM diagnosis, 75 years compared to 69 years of age (Figure 1; Table 1).

The risk of death was significantly increased for those with a known comorbidity at MM diagnosis (HR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.29-1.40). Having one comorbidity at diagnosis increased the risk of death by 19% (HR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.14-1.25), and having two and three or more comorbid diseases at diagnosis increased the risk of death incrementally (HR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.30-1.47 and HR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.62-1.83, respectively, Figures 1 and 2). The difference between these four groups was statistically significant, P < .001 (Figure 1).

The risk of death was significantly increased among patients with 14 comorbidities out of the 21 that were defined (Figure 2). The risk was highest for patients with dementia at MM diagnosis (HR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.45-2.04), followed by patients with chronic heart failure (HR = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.44-1.66). The risk was significantly increased for patients with prior history of inflammatory bowel disease (HR = 1.35, 95% CI: 1.04-1.76), psychological disease (1.30; 1.19-1.42), liver disease (1.22; 1.03-1.45), chronic lung disease (1.21; 1.11-1.31), chronic kidney disease (1.20; 1.00-1.43), peripheral vascular disease (1.20; 1.07-1.35), peptic ulcer (1.20; 1.09-1.32), neurological disease (1.17; 1.06-1.31), cerebrovascular disease (1.20; 1.11-1.29), diabetes mellitus (1.11; 1.03-1.20), arrhythmia (1.10; 1.03-1.17), and cancer (1.12; 1.05-1.19). Other diseases at diagnosis did not affect survival and only three patients were diagnosed with HIV and HIV therefore excluded from the survival analysis (Figure 2).

The median overall survival for patients with comorbidity at diagnosis was 2.4 years, (95% CI: 2.3-2.5) and 3.8 years (95% CI: 3.7-3.9) for patients without a comorbid condition (P < .001). Those patients with a known comorbidity at diagnosis were more likely to die from any other cause than MM, with an odds ratio of 1.56 (95% CI: 1.32-1.84) for those with one comorbidity, and 1.89 (95% CI: 1.56-2.28) and 2.44 (95% CI: 2.03-2.93) for those with two comorbidities and more than three comorbidities at diagnosis, respectively (Table 2).

In the sensitivity analysis comparing the 21 groups of diseases identified in relation to calendar periods 1990-1999 and 2000-2013, there was no difference in the risk of death among patients with and without comorbidities except for patients with chronic kidney disease. The risk of death was higher for the patient group diagnosed with chronic kidney disease in 1990-1999 (HR = 1.75, 95% CI: 1.27-2.42) compared to 2000-2013 (HR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.86-1.30). This was confirmed by interaction analysis showing a higher risk in the former period compared to the later era (HR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.19-2.57). Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis comparing the calendar period 2000-2006 to 2007-2013 did not show any difference in risk of death except for patients with cerebrovascular disease, where the risk became insignificant in the later period (data not shown). In addition, there was no change in overall risk of death when patients with comorbidities at diagnosis were compared to those without comorbid conditions (data not shown).

When analyzing inpatient diagnosis only, no significant changes in risk of death were observed compared to using both inpatient and outpatient data in those 21 diseases that were identified (data not shown). In total, 6797 (50.4%) patients in the inpatient registry had a comorbidity at diagnosis, compared to 54.0% using both inpatient and outpatient registries. The change in risk for patients with chronic kidney disease was the same as before, with a reduce in risk in the later time period (HR = 1.74, 95% CI: 1.26-2.41 for 1990-1999 and HR = 1.13, 95% CI: 0.90-1.43 for 2000-2013). This was also confirmed by interaction analysis, with a higher risk for the former era (HR = 1.59, 95% CI: 1.07-2.38).

The risk of death for patients 70 years of age and older with a comorbidity at diagnosis compared to those without a comorbidity was 41% higher (HR = 1.41, 95% CI: 1.34 - 1.49) and for patients younger than 70 years the risk was 46% increased (HR = 1.46, 95% CI: 1.36 - 1.56). Both older and younger patients had a significant step-wise increase in the risk of death in relation to the number of comorbidities at diagnosis (Figure 3A-B). A sensitivity analysis was performed comparing the groups when comorbidities were counted at diagnosis and no difference was found (data not shown). However, when estimating the risk of the 21 diseases identified, a difference was observed in patients with arrhythmia where younger patients had a significantly higher risk of death compared to patients 70 years of age and older (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.19 - 1.66 and HR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.06 - 1.22, respectively). The risk was therefore lower for the older age group, confirmed by the interaction analysis (HR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.70 - 0.99) No other significant differences were between the age groups.

## 4 Discussion

In this large population-based study including over 13,000 patients with MM diagnosed in Sweden over a period of 23 years, and detailed information of all of their significant comorbidities, we demonstrated that over 50% patients with a newly diagnosed MM have at least one comorbidity at diagnosis. Importantly, our study shows that MM patients with comorbidities present at diagnosis have 33% higher risk of death compared to those without a comorbid condition. In addition, our results show that 14 disease categories are related to worse survival. These findings emphasize the importance of comorbidities in MM, especially as frail patients with comorbidities are often excluded from RCTs. \[33\]

The prevalence of comorbidity at diagnosis was 54% in the current study, higher than in a recent study from Denmark that only utilized diagnoses compatible with the Charlson comorbidity index. \[19,25\] Due to our thorough approach using registry data, we include important comorbidities that have, to our knowledge, not been studied before, such as psychological diseases which are known to decrease survival in the general population as well as among cancer patients. \[27,31\] The prevalence of each disease was similar to previous studies, with hypertension being the most common comorbidity, followed by heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and a previous malignancy. \[11,17,19,34\] In our study, patients with a known comorbidity were older at the time of diagnosis compared to those without a comorbid condition; however, a total of 40% were under the age of 70 years, indicating the presence and importance of comorbidities in younger patients.

Our findings demonstrate that having any comorbidity at MM diagnosis, increases the risk of death by 34% compared to those patients without a comorbidity at diagnosis. Furthermore, there was an apparent additive effect of the number of comorbidities on survival. Importantly, this relationship was preserved for both older and younger patients, with a step-wise increase in the risk of death for each contributing comorbidity. The presence of comorbidity might affect treatment choices and therefore reduce survival, as has been shown in younger patients in Denmark, where a marked reduction in high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell transplant among younger patients with many comorbidities was observed. \[19\] This underlines the importance of assessing each patient at diagnosis, especially regarding the presence of comorbidities in the patients’ medical history, as patients with a known comorbidity might be more vulnerable to treatment and prone to adverse effects which might in turn influence the overall survival. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has even shed a light on the importance of comorbidities, where up to 75% MM patients who got infected by the virus and admitted to hospital had a comorbidity at diagnosis, and over 80% of patients who died from COVID suffered from other diseases than MM. \[35\]

In the current study, 14 diseases were related to a higher risk of death. Patients with dementia had the highest risk of death (72% higher), followed by heart failure which increased the risk by 54%. This is in accordance with a prior smaller study \[19\] among patients with MM as well as other studies the general population. \[36,37\] Interestingly, in our study, having a history of a mental disorder increased the risk of death 1.3-fold. This, to our knowledge, has not been reported before in MM patients, but survival among cancer patients with psychological diseases is known to be decreased. \[31\] Additionally, the risk was increased in those with a history of inflammatory bowel disease, peptic ulcer disease, neurological disease, liver disease, chronic lung disease, chronic kidney disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, cancer, diabetes mellitus, and arrhythmia with a moderate risk increase, similar to previous reports on MM patients \[14,19\] as well as in patients with cancer. \[28-30\] Interestingly, history of peptic ulcer decreases survival in the general population, which seems to be explained by frailty, treatment-related events, and comorbidities that go in hand with a history of peptic ulcer. \[38\] Similarly, the diagnosis of arrhythmia increases the risk of death in the general population \[39,40\]; in the current study, this was true for patients <70 years when compared to >70 years of age probably reflecting more severe underlying heart disease-causing arrythmia in younger patients. History of ischemic heart disease did not increase the risk of death in MM patients, reflecting advances in treatment and survival in the past decades. \[41\] Rheumatologic disease did not increase the risk of death; however, in a sub-analysis, the risk of death was significantly increased for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. To assess this further, these diseases were used instead of the disease group of rheumatoid diseases. When correcting for other diseases as well as age, year of diagnosis, and gender, this risk became non-significant. Taken together, the effect of comorbidities on survival in MM patients underlines the complexity of evaluating newly diagnosed patients, with the possibility of both under-treating by a dose-reduction or increasing the risk of treatment-related conditions such as infection or thrombosis.

The presence of a kidney disease is well known to have an impact on survival in MM, and it is often a challenge to distinguish between a comorbidity or myeloma-kidney disease. \[16,20\] In our study, we only included patients with a known kidney disease at least six months before the diagnosis of MM, reducing the risk of misclassification. In the analyses on calendar period, chronic kidney disease was the only comorbidity that was different between these periods, and patients with chronic kidney disease had a significantly lower risk of death in the more recent years. This difference remained when outpatient diagnosis where excluded. The most likely explanation is that after 2000, more effective treatment for MM emerged. \[4,6,24\] Novel drugs were increasingly used in Sweden, with up to 80% of patients receiving one of these drugs in 2013. \[7\] In particular, bortezomib has been shown to reduce tumor burden and improve renal response, and is the drug of choice in renal failure. \[42\] Immunomodulatory drugs such as lenalidomide (requires dose-adjustment according to creatinine clearance) and pomalidomide are also safe for this patient group. \[42\] Furthermore, the management of chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease has improved in the last decades with a reduction in mortality rate among these patients. \[43\] Therefore, the decrease in risk of death in this group can represent more aggressive and better treatment of these individuals in the latter calendar period. To further evaluate the effect of novel therapies, an analysis of the later calendar period was performed, comparing the years 2000-2006 to 2007-2013. There was no difference in risk of death except for patients with a known diagnosis of cerebrovascular disease where the risk became non-significant in the later calendar period. This correlates to the recent trends in mortality and improved survival among patients with cerebrovascular disease. \[44\] However, there was no other difference between these calendar periods, both in risk of death and overall survival, despite a steep increase in the use of novel treatments, such as the immunomodulary drugs in the later era. This might be explained by the short follow-up time of patients and the impact of treatments need to be studied further as no information on individual treatments was available in this study.

In the cause of death analysis, 11% of patients did not have MM listed as a cause of death which is similar to a recent European study. \[45\] Furthermore, a higher number of comorbidities at diagnosis gave higher odds of dying from other causes than myeloma. A recent Spanish study \[46\] on early mortality yielded similar results, with comorbidities such as liver disease, respiratory disease, and hepatitis C infection, all contributing to an early mortality. This emphasizes even more the complexity of comorbidity at diagnosis and the challenge it poses in relation to treatment decisions and patient evaluation.

Our study possesses several strengths. First, it is nationwide and includes all patients diagnosed with MM in Sweden over a period of 23 years. The data are collected from a stable population which has access to standardized universal health care with high completeness and validity of the Swedish Cancer Registry. \[22\] The use of real-world data ensures that our cohort reflects a whole patient population. Additionally, using the Swedish Patient Registry, we are able to capture every diagnosis both from inpatient data and from outpatient registries for each patient in the years leading up to the MM diagnosis. As every individual has a unique identification number, we have an extensive and accurate follow-up for all patients included in the study. Furthermore, the application of a register-based cohort design minimized recall-bias and the high number of patients included yielded high statistical power.

The limitations of our study include lack of information on clinical stage, laboratory data, and treatment of each individual, making it difficult to evaluate if the presence of comorbidities influenced individual treatment choices or was associated with higher risk of adverse events. This is of particular importance among older individuals who have more comorbidities and do not receive a high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell transplantation. In addition, outpatient data were only available from the year 2000, which might underestimate the prevalence and risk of each comorbidity. However, sensitivity analysis based only on patients diagnosed after the year 2000 showed no difference between the calendar periods (data not shown). Furthermore, information on obesity was based on ICD diagnosis which is not widespread and not based on the body mass index of patients. Unfortunately, we do not have access to this data and it is therefore likely that we have not captured all obesity diagnoses.

In conclusion, our results show that 50% of newly diagnosed MM patients have at least one comorbidity and that it impairs overall survival when compared to patients without a known comorbidity, even showing an increased impact relating to the number of comorbid conditions. Our results are clinically important as we show that newly diagnosed MM patients with an underlying comorbidity have a significantly shorter overall survival (median 3.8 vs 2.4 years, respectively) compared to newly diagnosed MM patients without a comorbid condition. Furthermore, our results address the significance of evaluating each patient at diagnosis with proper risk stratification, including a detailed medical history as the presence of comorbidity may increase the risk of adverse effects and result in less aggressive treatment regimens, with both leading to inferior survival in MM.

# Comorbidities in multiple myeloma and implications on survival: A population-based study

Ingigerður S. Sverrisdóttir (1); Sölvi Rögnvaldsson (1); Sigrún Thorsteinsdottir (1); Gauti K. Gíslason (1); Thor Aspelund (1); Ingemar Turesson (2); Magnus Björkholm (3); Henrik Gregersen (4); Cecilie Hveding Blimark (5); Ola Landgren (6); Sigurður Y. Kristinsson (1,7)

**Original Article** — DOI: 10.1111/ejh.13597

© 2021 John Wiley & Sons A/S. Published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd

Received: 3 December 2020 | Revised: 4 February 2021 | Accepted: 8 February 2021

## Affiliations

1. Faculty of Medicine, University of Iceland, Reykjavík, Iceland
2. University Hospital Malmö, Malmö, Sweden
3. Division of Haematology, Department of Medicine, Karolinska University Hospital and Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden
4. Department of Haematology, Aalborg University Hospital, Aalborg, Denmark
5. Department of Haematology, Sahlgrenska University Hospital and Institution of Internal Medicine, Sahlgrenska Academy at University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden
6. Myeloma Program, Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of Miami, Miami, FL, USA
7. Department of Haematology, Landspitali National University Hospital, Reykjavik, Iceland

**Correspondence:** Ingigerður S Sverrisdóttir, Faculty of Medicine, University of Iceland, Sturlugötu 8, 101 Reykjavik, Iceland. Email: [ingigerdursverrisdottir@gmail.com](mailto:ingigerdursverrisdottir@gmail.com)

## Abstract

High proportion of patients with multiple myeloma suffer from comorbidities which may alter clinical management. Therefore, our aims were to evaluate the prevalence of comorbidities and their impact on survival. We included patients diagnosed with multiple myeloma 1990-2013 in Sweden and all diagnoses from each patient from 1985. A total of 13 656 patients with multiple myeloma were included in the study, thereof 7404 (54%) had comorbidity at diagnosis. The risk of death was increased for those with one comorbidity at diagnosis compared to those without any comorbidity (hazard ratio = 1.19; 95% confidence interval:1.14-1.25); this risk was higher for those with two (1.38; 1.30-1.47) and three or more comorbidities (1.72; 1.62-1.83). Furthermore, the risk of death was increased in patients with prior history of cancer, arrhythmia, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, cerebrovascular disease, chronic lung disease, psychological disease, peptic ulcer, neurological disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic kidney disease, dementia, and inflammatory bowel disease. This large study shows that over 50% of multiple myeloma patients have a comorbidity at diagnosis and survival decreased with increasing numbers of comorbidities. This emphasizes the importance of comorbidities when evaluating patients and deciding on treatment strategies for individuals with multiple myeloma.

**Keywords:** comorbidities, multiple myeloma, survival

## 1 Introduction

Multiple myeloma (MM) is a plasma-cell malignancy that affects approximately 160,000 individuals annually world-wide. \[1\] The median age at diagnosis is around 70 years, 5%-10% of patients are diagnosed below 50 years of age, with a lower prevalence of young patients in population-based studies. \[2,3\] With an aging population and prolonged survival, the incidence and prevalence of MM are increasing \[4-7\] and elderly patients are more likely to suffer from comorbid conditions. \[8,9\]

Comorbidities may influence cancer detection, treatment, progression, and thereby prognosis of each patient. \[10,11\] In MM patients, comorbid diseases may lead to lower performance status, decreased quality of life, and life-threatening conditions. \[12,13\] We have recently shown that concurrent autoimmune disease and thrombosis is associated with inferior survival in MM patients. \[14,15\] Despite the importance of considering comorbid diseases in the treatment and prognosis of MM, the literature on comorbidity in MM is limited and based on small numbers. \[16-20\]

New therapeutic agents with different mechanisms of action, such as lenalidomide, pomalidomide, daratumumab, and carfilzomib, \[21\] have been shown to improve survival in randomized clinical trials (RCTs); however, there are very few clinical trials where elderly and frail patients are included. \[12\] Patients with comorbidities are typically not eligible for enrollment in clinical trials, and, consequently, there is limited information available on comorbidities in MM and implications on clinical outcomes. Therefore, it is of great importance to evaluate comorbidity in MM, in particular using real-world data.

Aims of our study were to evaluate the prevalence of comorbidity and the effect of comorbid conditions on survival in a whole population using real-world data among more than 13 000 newly diagnosed MM patients in Sweden over a period of 23 years.

## 2 Methods

### 2.1 Cohort and registries

All residents of Sweden are, at birth or immigration, assigned a unique personal identification number that is used in government-maintained nationwide health care and population registers, whereby medical record linkage is possible with a high degree of accuracy.

The Swedish Cancer Registry is a centralized, nationwide registry that contains information on patients diagnosed with a malignant disorder in Sweden since January 1, 1958 (completeness >93% for MM patients). \[22\] Using this registry, patients diagnosed with MM from January 1, 1990, to December 31, 2013, were identified.

Using International Code of Diseases (ICD)-10 and ICD-9 codes, a total of 21 disease groups were identified (Table S1). The formation of these groups is explained below. Information on each patient was gathered from the Swedish Patient registry, which contains inpatient data from 1987 as well as information on outpatient visits from 2000. \[23\] All chronic diseases that were diagnosed up to 10 years before the diagnosis of MM were included in the analysis. Diagnosis of comorbid diseases had to be made before the MM diagnosis or a maximum of 30 days after diagnosis with the exception of inflammatory bowel disease, renal, and rheumatological disease. These conditions had to be diagnosed at least half a year before as symptoms of MM might mimic these diseases and lead to a wrong diagnosis. In a sensitivity analysis, we removed all diagnosis up to four weeks prior to the MM diagnosis and risk estimates for each disease remained the same (data not shown). Information on prior cancer diagnoses was obtained from the Swedish Cancer Registry. All cancer diagnoses up to 10 years prior to diagnosis of MM were identified, excluding benign tumors as well as cancer in situ.

End of follow-up was December 31, 2013. The study period was divided into two calendar periods, 1990-1999 and 2000-2013, before and after the introduction of novel treatment options for MM in Sweden. \[6,24\] Information on date of death as well as cause of death was obtained from the centralized Swedish Cause of Death Registry. In evaluating the cause of death, the data were split into those who had MM listed as any cause of death and those without a MM diagnosis in the Cause of Death Registry.

### 2.2 Comorbidity

A total of 65 diseases were identified using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes from the Swedish Patient Registry, using both inpatient and outpatient data. These diseases were grouped together according to previously published data, both the Charlson comorbidity index as well as newly published study from Denmark. \[19,25\] Certain diseases that are not evaluated in the Charlson index were added to capture as many comorbidities as possible, specifically those known to effect survival in the general population as well as the survival of patients with known cancer. \[14,26-31\] In total, psychological disorders, neurological conditions, arrhythmias, pancreatic disease, inflammatory bowel disease, hypertension, and obesity were added. The diseases listed were chronic in nature and typically need lifelong follow-up or treatment.

ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes were used to identify each diagnosis in the corresponding groups, and these codes were based on ICD-9 and ICD-10 versions of the Charlson index. \[32\] In order to group these 65 diseases together, we conducted a separate analysis where all 65 diseases were evaluated independently for their risk of death. Diseases were grouped together according to their ICD-10 classification as well as the organ or organ systems that were affected by the disease. After ICD and organ system classification, diseases were grouped together if the risk of death was similar. A disease was only added to a group if the risk was alike or did not change when the disease was added to that specific category. Altogether, a total of 21 disease groups were defined. Table S1 shows the diseases groups and which diagnosis were included with corresponding ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes for each group.

### 2.3 Statistical analysis

We estimated the effect of comorbidities on the risk of death for patients with MM using two different Cox regression models. The first model included only the number of comorbidities present at diagnosis and the second model included all of the 21 comorbidities we identified. Both models were adjusted for age, sex, and year of diagnosis with age and year of diagnosis as continuous variables. Results were presented as hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Kaplan-Meier curves were used to estimate survival with respect to the number of comorbidities present at diagnosis.

We also looked at all subjects that died during the study period, and cross-linked them to the Cause of Death Registry. Using logistic regression, we evaluated the odds of dying from other causes than MM depending on the number of comorbidities present at diagnosis, with the same adjustment variables as above. Results were presented as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

As the outpatient diagnosis was only available from the year 2000, a sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate if there was any difference in the risk of each comorbidity between two calendar periods, 1990-1999 and 2000-2013. This was done by adding an interaction term between each comorbidity and the time period variable to the Cox model. For further comparison, we fitted a separate Cox model only on inpatient diagnoses to evaluate if the hazard ratios changed when outpatient diagnoses were excluded. To assess the interaction between the risk of each comorbidity and age at diagnosis, we stratified the group into patients older and younger than 70 years of age and fitted a Cox model for each age group separately as well as adding an interaction term between each comorbidity and the age group variable.

Statistical significance was set at P < .05, all confidence intervals were 95%, and all statistical analyses were performed in R version 3.6.1.

## 3 Results

In total, 13 656 patients were diagnosed with MM in the Swedish Cancer Registry from the January 1, 1990, to the December 31, 2013. The median age of diagnosis was 72 years (20-99), and 7481 (54.8%) were male. Around 60% of patients were older than 70 years at the time of MM diagnosis, and 63% of these older patients had a comorbidity at diagnosis (Table 1).

A total of 7404 (54.2%) patients had one or more comorbidity at MM diagnosis, and the most common comorbidities were hypertension (20.4%), cancer (11.3%), arrhythmia (11.3%), and chronic ischemic heart disease (9.2%). Other comorbidities and their prevalence are shown in Figure 1. Of all patients, 3355 (24.6%) had only one comorbidity listed at the MM diagnosis, 1922 (14.1%) had two comorbidities, and 2126 (15.6%) had three or more comorbidities at diagnosis. More patients were diagnosed with MM and concurrent comorbidities during the calendar period 2000-2013 (61.7%) compared to 1990-1999 (38.3%), and patients with comorbidities were older at the time of MM diagnosis, 75 years compared to 69 years of age (Figure 1; Table 1).

The risk of death was significantly increased for those with a known comorbidity at MM diagnosis (HR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.29-1.40). The risk of death was significantly increased among patients with 14 comorbidities out of the 21 that were defined (Figure 2). The risk was highest for patients with dementia at MM diagnosis (HR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.45-2.04), followed by patients with chronic heart failure (HR = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.44-1.66). In the sensitivity analysis comparing the 21 groups of diseases identified in relation to calendar periods 1990-1999 and 2000-2013, there was no difference in the risk of death among patients with and without comorbidities except for patients with chronic kidney disease. The risk of death was higher for the patient group diagnosed with chronic kidney disease in 1990-1999 (HR = 1.75, 95% CI: 1.27-2.42) compared to 2000-2013 (HR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.86-1.30). This was confirmed by interaction analysis showing a higher risk in the former period compared to the later era (HR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.19-2.57). Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis comparing the calendar period 2000-2006 to 2007-2013 did not show any difference in risk of death except for patients with cerebrovascular disease, where the risk became insignificant in the later period (data not shown). In addition, there was no change in overall risk of death when patients with comorbidities at diagnosis were compared to those without comorbid conditions (data not shown).

When analyzing inpatient diagnosis only, no significant changes in risk of death were observed compared to using both inpatient and outpatient data in those 21 diseases that were identified (data not shown). In total, 6797 (50.4%) patients in the inpatient registry had a comorbidity at diagnosis, compared to 54.0% using both inpatient and outpatient registries. The change in risk for patients with chronic kidney disease was the same as before, with a reduce in risk in the later time period (HR = 1.74, 95% CI: 1.26-2.41 for 1990-1999 and HR = 1.13, 95% CI: 0.90-1.43 for 2000-2013). This was also confirmed by interaction analysis, with a higher risk for the former era (HR = 1.59, 95% CI: 1.07-2.38).

The risk of death for patients 70 years of age and older with a comorbidity at diagnosis compared to those without a comorbidity was 41% higher (HR = 1.41, 95% CI: 1.34 - 1.49) and for patients younger than 70 years the risk was 46% increased (HR = 1.46, 95% CI: 1.36 - 1.56). Both older and younger patients had a significant step-wise increase in the risk of death in relation to the number of comorbidities at diagnosis (Figure 3A-B). A sensitivity analysis was performed comparing the groups when comorbidities were counted at diagnosis and no difference was found (data not shown). However, when estimating the risk of the 21 diseases identified, a difference was observed in patients with arrhythmia where younger patients had a significantly higher risk of death compared to patients 70 years of age and older (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.19 - 1.66 and HR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.06 - 1.22, respectively). The risk was therefore lower for the older age group, confirmed by the interaction analysis (HR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.70 - 0.99) No other significant differences were between the age groups.

## 4 Discussion

In this large population-based study including over 13,000 patients with MM diagnosed in Sweden over a period of 23 years, and detailed information of all of their significant comorbidities, we demonstrated that over 50% patients with a newly diagnosed MM have at least one comorbidity at diagnosis. Importantly, our study shows that MM patients with comorbidities present at diagnosis have 33% higher risk of death compared to those without a comorbid condition. In addition, our results show that 14 disease categories are related to worse survival. These findings emphasize the importance of comorbidities in MM, especially as frail patients with comorbidities are often excluded from RCTs. \[33\]

The prevalence of comorbidity at diagnosis was 54% in the current study, higher than in a recent study from Denmark that only utilized diagnoses compatible with the Charlson comorbidity index. \[19,25\] Due to our thorough approach using registry data, we include important comorbidities that have, to our knowledge, not been studied before, such as psychological diseases which are known to decrease survival in the general population as well as among cancer patients. \[27,31\] The prevalence of each disease was similar to previous studies, with hypertension being the most common comorbidity, followed by heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and a previous malignancy. \[11,17,19,34\] In our study, patients with a known comorbidity were older at the time of diagnosis compared to those without a comorbid condition; however, a total of 40% were under the age of 70 years, indicating the presence and importance of comorbidities in younger patients.

Our findings demonstrate that having any comorbidity at MM diagnosis, increases the risk of death by 34% compared to those patients without a comorbidity at diagnosis. Furthermore, there was an apparent additive effect of the number of comorbidities on survival. Importantly, this relationship was preserved for both older and younger patients, with a step-wise increase in the risk of death for each contributing comorbidity. The presence of comorbidity might affect treatment choices and therefore reduce survival, as has been shown in younger patients in Denmark, where a marked reduction in high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell transplant among younger patients with many comorbidities was observed. \[19\] This underlines the importance of assessing each patient at diagnosis, especially regarding the presence of comorbidities in the patients’ medical history, as patients with a known comorbidity might be more vulnerable to treatment and prone to adverse effects which might in turn influence the overall survival. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has even shed a light on the importance of comorbidities, where up to 75% MM patients who got infected by the virus and admitted to hospital had a comorbidity at diagnosis, and over 80% of patients who died from COVID suffered from other diseases than MM. \[35\]

In the current study, 14 diseases were related to a higher risk of death. Patients with dementia had the highest risk of death (72% higher), followed by heart failure which increased the risk by 54%. This is in accordance with a prior smaller study \[19\] among patients with MM as well as other studies the general population. \[36,37\] Interestingly, in our study, having a history of a mental disorder increased the risk of death 1.3-fold. This, to our knowledge, has not been reported before in MM patients, but survival among cancer patients with psychological diseases is known to be decreased. \[31\] Additionally, the risk was increased in those with a history of inflammatory bowel disease, peptic ulcer disease, neurological disease, liver disease, chronic lung disease, chronic kidney disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, cancer, diabetes mellitus, and arrhythmia with a moderate risk increase, similar to previous reports on MM patients \[14,19\] as well as in patients with cancer. \[28-30\] Interestingly, history of peptic ulcer decreases survival in the general population, which seems to be explained by frailty, treatment-related events, and comorbidities that go in hand with a history of peptic ulcer. \[38\] Similarly, the diagnosis of arrhythmia increases the risk of death in the general population \[39,40\]; in the current study, this was true for patients <70 years when compared to >70 years of age probably reflecting more severe underlying heart disease-causing arrythmia in younger patients. History of ischemic heart disease did not increase the risk of death in MM patients, reflecting advances in treatment and survival in the past decades. \[41\] Rheumatologic disease did not increase the risk of death; however, in a sub-analysis, the risk of death was significantly increased for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. To assess this further, these diseases were used instead of the disease group of rheumatoid diseases. When correcting for other diseases as well as age, year of diagnosis, and gender, this risk became non-significant. Taken together, the effect of comorbidities on survival in MM patients underlines the complexity of evaluating newly diagnosed patients, with the possibility of both under-treating by a dose-reduction or increasing the risk of treatment-related conditions such as infection or thrombosis.

The presence of a kidney disease is well known to have an impact on survival in MM, and it is often a challenge to distinguish between a comorbidity or myeloma-kidney disease. \[16,20\] In our study, we only included patients with a known kidney disease at least six months before the diagnosis of MM, reducing the risk of misclassification. In the analyses on calendar period, chronic kidney disease was the only comorbidity that was different between these periods, and patients with chronic kidney disease had a significantly lower risk of death in the more recent years. This difference remained when outpatient diagnosis where excluded. The most likely explanation is that after 2000, more effective treatment for MM emerged. \[4,6,24\] Novel drugs were increasingly used in Sweden, with up to 80% of patients receiving one of these drugs in 2013. \[7\] In particular, bortezomib has been shown to reduce tumor burden and improve renal response, and is the drug of choice in renal failure. \[42\] Immunomodulatory drugs such as lenalidomide (requires dose-adjustment according to creatinine clearance) and pomalidomide are also safe for this patient group. \[42\] Furthermore, the management of chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease has improved in the last decades with a reduction in mortality rate among these patients. \[43\] Therefore, the decrease in risk of death in this group can represent more aggressive and better treatment of these individuals in the latter calendar period. To further evaluate the effect of novel therapies, an analysis of the later calendar period was performed, comparing the years 2000-2006 to 2007-2013. There was no difference in risk of death except for patients with a known diagnosis of cerebrovascular disease where the risk became non-significant in the later calendar period. This correlates to the recent trends in mortality and improved survival among patients with cerebrovascular disease. \[44\] However, there was no other difference between these calendar periods, both in risk of death and overall survival, despite a steep increase in the use of novel treatments, such as the immunomodulary drugs in the later era. This might be explained by the short follow-up time of patients and the impact of treatments need to be studied further as no information on individual treatments was available in this study.

In the cause of death analysis, 11% of patients did not have MM listed as a cause of death which is similar to a recent European study. \[45\] Furthermore, a higher number of comorbidities at diagnosis gave higher odds of dying from other causes than myeloma. A recent Spanish study \[46\] on early mortality yielded similar results, with comorbidities such as liver disease, respiratory disease, and hepatitis C infection, all contributing to an early mortality. This emphasizes even more the complexity of comorbidity at diagnosis and the challenge it poses in relation to treatment decisions and patient evaluation.

Our study possesses several strengths. First, it is nationwide and includes all patients diagnosed with MM in Sweden over a period of 23 years. The data are collected from a stable population which has access to standardized universal health care with high completeness and validity of the Swedish Cancer Registry. \[22\] The use of real-world data ensures that our cohort reflects a whole patient population. Additionally, using the Swedish Patient Registry, we are able to capture every diagnosis both from inpatient data and from outpatient registries for each patient in the years leading up to the MM diagnosis. As every individual has a unique identification number, we have an extensive and accurate follow-up for all patients included in the study. Furthermore, the application of a register-based cohort design minimized recall-bias and the high number of patients included yielded high statistical power.

The limitations of our study include lack of information on clinical stage, laboratory data, and treatment of each individual, making it difficult to evaluate if the presence of comorbidities influenced individual treatment choices or was associated with higher risk of adverse events. This is of particular importance among older individuals who have more comorbidities and do not receive a high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell transplantation. In addition, outpatient data were only available from the year 2000, which might underestimate the prevalence and risk of each comorbidity. However, sensitivity analysis based only on patients diagnosed after the year 2000 showed no difference between the calendar periods (data not shown). Furthermore, information on obesity was based on ICD diagnosis which is not widespread and not based on the body mass index of patients. Unfortunately, we do not have access to this data and it is therefore likely that we have not captured all obesity diagnoses.

In conclusion, our results show that 50% of newly diagnosed MM patients have at least one comorbidity and that it impairs overall survival when compared to patients without a known comorbidity, even showing an increased impact relating to the number of comorbid conditions. Our results are clinically important as we show that newly diagnosed MM patients with an underlying comorbidity have a significantly shorter overall survival (median 3.8 vs 2.4 years, respectively) compared to newly diagnosed MM patients without a comorbid condition. Furthermore, our results address the significance of evaluating each patient at diagnosis with proper risk stratification, including a detailed medical history as the presence of comorbidity may increase the risk of adverse effects and result in less aggressive treatment regimens, with both leading to inferior survival in MM.
